content_html:
Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one, usually to get a lower rate, change the term or take cash out of your home equity. A lower payment is only part of the story. Closing costs have to be recovered, and resetting the clock on a loan can mean paying interest for more years. This calculator compares both loans side by side so you can see the trade-off in dollars.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current loan: enter the remaining balance from your latest statement, your current interest rate and how long is left on the loan. The calculator works out your current principal and interest payment from these.
  2. New loan: enter the quoted rate and the term you are considering.
  3. Points: one point is a fee of 1% of the new loan amount, usually paid to buy a lower rate.
  4. Other closing costs: appraisal, title insurance, origination and recording fees from your loan estimate.
  5. More options: add cash out, or roll the closing costs into the new loan instead of paying them at closing.

What the results mean

  • Monthly payment change: the current payment minus the new one. Only principal and interest are compared, because taxes and insurance stay the same either way.
  • Break-even: closing costs divided by the monthly saving, rounded up to a whole month. If you expect to sell or refinance again before then, the refinance is likely to cost more than it saves.
  • Over the life of both loans: every remaining payment on the current loan compared with every payment on the new loan plus costs paid at closing.

Payments use the standard fixed-rate formula, M = L × i / (1 − (1 + i)−n), where i is the yearly rate divided by 12 and n the number of months. When you roll costs into the loan, the points are charged on the larger final loan amount.

A worked example

Suppose you owe $250,000 at 7% with 25 years left, and a lender offers 6% on a new 30-year loan with 1 point and $3,000 of other costs, so $5,500 in total:

 Current loanNew 30-year loanNew 25-year loan
Monthly payment$1,766.95$1,498.88$1,610.75
Monthly saving–$268.07$156.19
Break-even–21 months36 months
Lifetime result–$15,011.07 more$41,358.35 saved

The 30-year loan has the bigger monthly saving, but because it adds five years of payments it costs more in total. Matching the new term to the 25 years you have left keeps most of the rate benefit.

Things to weigh before refinancing

  • How long you will stay. The break-even point matters most if you might move in a few years.
  • The term you choose. A shorter term raises the payment but can save far more interest than a lower rate alone.
  • Cash out costs money. Borrowing against your home adds to the balance and the interest, and the savings shown here do not count the cash you receive.
  • Points are optional. Compare a no-points quote with a points quote; paying points only pays off if you keep the loan long enough.
  • Prepayment instead. Putting the closing costs toward your current principal is another option worth comparing.

faq.question: How much lower should my rate be to refinance?
faq.answer: There is no fixed rule. What matters is whether the monthly saving recovers your closing costs well before you expect to sell or refinance again, which is what the break-even figure shows.

faq.question: Can I refinance with no closing costs?
faq.answer: Some lenders offer no-closing-cost loans, but they usually charge a higher rate or add the costs to the balance. Use the roll-in option to see the effect of borrowing the costs, or enter a slightly higher rate with zero costs.

faq.question: Does refinancing restart my loan?
faq.answer: Yes. The new loan starts a fresh term. Choosing a term no longer than the time left on your current loan avoids stretching out your payments.

faq.question: Are taxes and insurance included?
faq.answer: No. Property tax and homeowners insurance generally stay the same when you refinance, so the comparison uses principal and interest only. Mortgage insurance can change, so check your loan estimate if you pay it.

faq.question: Can I use this for car or personal loans?
faq.answer: Yes. The same comparison works for any fixed-rate installment loan. Enter the balance, rate and time left on your current loan and the terms of the new one.
